claims.source: Inhibitory synaptic responses could significantly boost STO amplitude (ΔSTO amplitude of first cycle 4.8±3.7 mV, p<0.0001; second cycle 1.0±1.7 mV, p<0.0001; third cycle 0.57±1.7 mV, p<0.0001; fourth cycle 0.4±1.3 mV, n=24, N=19; p=0.0002, Friedman test) (Figure 2I).
claims.evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 2I with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Olivary synaptic responses to excitatory input from the MDJ are comprised of a depolarization mediated by AMPA and NMDA receptors.
claims.source: Olivary synaptic responses to excitatory input from the MDJ are comprised of a depolarization (Vdep) mediated by AMPA and NMDA receptors (Mathy et al., 2014; Turecek et al., 2014), followed by a hyperpolarization (Vhyp), mediated by both HCN and SK channels (Garden et al., 2017; Garden et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Mathy et al., 2014; Turecek et al., 2014; Garden et al., 2017; and Garden et al., 2018.

claims.claim: The hyperpolarization following MDJ excitation is mediated by both HCN and SK channels.
claims.source: Olivary synaptic responses to excitatory input from the MDJ are comprised of a depolarization (Vdep) mediated by AMPA and NMDA receptors (Mathy et al., 2014; Turecek et al., 2014), followed by a hyperpolarization (Vhyp), mediated by both HCN and SK channels (Garden et al., 2017; Garden et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Garden et al., 2017 and Garden et al., 2018.

claims.claim: MDJ stimulation could only trigger STOs in intrinsically silent IO neurons when Vhyp was larger than ~3 mV.
claims.source: In general, stimulation of MDJ afferents could only trigger STOs in intrinsically silent IO neurons when Vhyp was larger than ~3 mV.
claims.evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from the study.

claims.claim: The duration of MDJ-induced transient oscillations (1.3±0.64 s) was significantly shorter than those occurring upon CN stimulation.
claims.source: The duration of these transient oscillations (1.3±0.64 s, ranging from 0.44 s to 2.36 s) was on average significantly shorter (p=0.005, unpaired t-test; n=6, N=5) than those occurring upon stimulation of the CN afferents.
claims.evidence: This is directly measured experimental data with statistical comparison.

claims.claim: MDJ stimulation induced a weak phase resetting in oscillating IO cells.
claims.source: Similarly, in oscillating IO cells, MDJ stimulation induced a weak phase resetting (Figure 3G) and significantly reduced the phase jitter (SDpost-stim=44.97 ms versus SDpre-stim=56.47 ms; p<0.0001, F test; n=16, N=14), but this latter reduction was significantly smaller (p<0.0001, F test) than that following CN stimulation (compare Figure 3F–H with Figure 2F–H).
claims.evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 3G with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: MDJ stimulation induced a relatively weak, yet significant, increase of the amplitude of post-stimulus oscillation cycles.
claims.source: Moreover, MDJ stimulation induced a relatively weak, yet significant, increase of the amplitude of the post-stimulus oscillation cycles in these cells (ΔSTO amplitude of first cycle 1.52±3.0 mV, p<0.0001; second cycle 0.60±2.0 mV, p<0.0001; third cycle 0.37±1.7 mV, p=0.01; fourth cycle 0.5±3.69 mV, p=0.0119; Friedman test, n=26, N=19), (Figure 3I).
claims.evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 3I with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Vhyp and Vreb were not significantly affected by picrotoxin following MDJ stimulation.
claims.source: Vhyp and Vreb were not significantly affected by the GABAA receptor antagonist picrotoxin (amplitude change relative to baseline, Vhyp: 138.1 ± 66.6%, p=0.1493; Vreb: 103.7 ± 36.5%, p=0.7852; n=8, N=8, paired t-test), whereas Vdep slightly increased (122.7 ± 13.92 %, p=0.0024) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and F).
claims.evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and F with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: CNQX prominently reduced all three components of the MDJ response.
claims.source: Instead, when AMPA receptors were blocked with CNQX all three components were prominently reduced (Vdep: 22.9 ± 12.18%, p<0.0001; Vhyp: 21.2 ± 19.7%, p<0.0001; Vreb: 10.8 ± 12.6%, p<0.0001; n=8, N=8, paired t-test).
claims.evidence: This is directly measured experimental data with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: APV caused a further reduction of all three components of the MDJ response after CNQX application.
claims.source: Moreover, application of the NMDA receptor antagonist APV (50 μM) caused a further reduction (Vdep: 7.0 ± 9.7%, p=0.001; Vhyp: 13.8 ± 17.4%, p=0.0022; Vreb: 7.2±14.4, p=0.001; n=4, N=4, paired t-test) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and F).
claims.evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and F with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: The IO model comprises over a thousand cells with inhibitory and excitatory arborizations from the CN and MDJ.
claims.source: In this work we have extended the IO model from Negrello et al., 2019, by scaling the number of cells to capture the murine MAO, comprising over a thousand cells with inhibitory and excitatory arborizations from the CN and MDJ, respectively (Vrieler et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This describes the computational model used in the study, supported by citation to Vrieler et al., 2019.

claims.claim: The network model can reproduce the strong phase resetting following CN stimulation observed experimentally.
claims.source: Indeed, both the strong phase resetting following CN stimulation (Figure 4A) and the relatively high variability in phase values following MDJ stimulation (Figure 4B) emerge from the model.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by modeling data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The network model can reproduce the relatively high variability in phase values following MDJ stimulation observed experimentally.
claims.source: Indeed, both the strong phase resetting following CN stimulation (Figure 4A) and the relatively high variability in phase values following MDJ stimulation (Figure 4B) emerge from the model.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by modeling data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The PRC slope did not differ significantly across most intervals tested, except for the condition where excitation followed inhibition by 150 ms.
claims.source: The PRC slope reflecting phase changes in relation to the phase of the STO during which stimulation occurred did not differ significantly across any of the intervals tested (Figure 5C and D), except for the condition where excitation followed inhibition by 150 ms (Figure 5E and F); for this interval the slope was significantly steeper (–0.69±0.05; p<0.0001, n=7, N=7, one-way ANOVA) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and C).
claims.evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figures 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: The ΔФ-intercept shifted significantly from a negative value at an interval of –100 ms to a positive value at an interval of 150 ms.
claims.source: Moreover, the ΔФ-intercept shifted significantly (p<0.0001, one-way ANOVA) from a negative value at an interval of –100 ms (i.e., excitation preceding inhibition; –0.16±0.02; n=6, N=4) to a positive value at an interval of 150 ms (0.35±0.03; n=7, N=7) (Figure 5C–F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B and D).
claims.evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: An interval of +150 ms yielded the highest STO amplitude of 7.25±3.45 mV during the first cycle.
claims.source: Indeed, whereas an interval of +150 ms yielded the highest STO amplitude of 7.25±3.45 mV during the first cycle (n=10, N=8), an interval of +50 ms resulted in an amplitude of only 1.83±3.42 mV (n=34, N=25) (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1G and H).
claims.evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: An interval of +50 ms resulted in an STO amplitude of only 1.83±3.42 mV.
claims.source: Indeed, whereas an interval of +150 ms yielded the highest STO amplitude of 7.25±3.45 mV during the first cycle (n=10, N=8), an interval of +50 ms resulted in an amplitude of only 1.83±3.42 mV (n=34, N=25) (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1G and H).
claims.evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: In the slice preparation, 57% of IO cells analyzed showed spontaneous spikes at a frequency of 0.1±0.1 Hz.
claims.source: Yet, in our slice preparation of the IO 57% of the cells analyzed (32 out of 56 neurons, N=36) showed spontaneous spikes at a significantly lower frequency of 0.1±0.1 Hz (ranging from 0.0017 to 0.34 Hz, membrane voltage range: from –56 to –41 mV).
claims.evidence: This is directly measured experimental data from the study.

claims.claim: In awake animals the spontaneous firing rate of complex spikes is approximately 1 Hz.
claims.source: In awake animals the spontaneous firing rate of complex spikes is approximately 1 Hz (Ju et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Ju et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Spike probability was low when excitation followed inhibition at intervals in the range of 50–70 ms.
claims.source: As expected, spike probability was low when excitation followed inhibition at intervals in the range of 50–70 ms (Pspike = 0 ± 0 in both cases; for 50 ms, n=9, N=8; for 70 ms, n=6, N=6), both near the trough of the hyperpolarizing component of the inhibitory response (Figures 5F and 6C).
claims.evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figures 5F and 6C.

claims.claim: Spike probability was largest at an interval of 150 ms (0.57±0.3).
claims.source: Spike probability was largest at an interval of 150 ms around the peak of the rebound component of the inhibitory response (0.57±0.3; n=9, N=8) (Figures 5F and 6C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1I and J), which coincides with the major resonant frequency of IO cells (Khosrovani et al., 2007; Negrello et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figures 5F and 6C with citations to Khosrovani et al., 2007 and Negrello et al., 2019.

claims.claim: The spike probability for the 150 ms interval was significantly higher than for either single inhibitory or excitatory responses.
claims.source: The spike probability for the 150 ms interval was significantly higher than for either single inhibitory (0.01±0.03, n=7, N=6; Figure 6A) or excitatory (0.22±0.28, n=7, N=6; Figure 6B) responses under the same Vm and stimulation strength (150 ms interval with respect to single inhibitory and single excitatory responses p<0.0001 and p=0.0018, respectively; one-way ANOVA) (Figures 5F and 6C, Figure 5—figure supplement1I and J).
claims.evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figures 5F and 6 with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: When focal stimulation of the excitatory input to a group of cells occurred one cycle after inhibition onset, the network produced the highest amplitude of rebound, largest spiking probability and effective phase resets.
claims.source: When focal stimulation of the excitatory input to a group of cells occurred one cycle after inhibition onset (cycle T=120 ms, 8 Hz), the network produced the highest amplitude of rebound, largest spiking probability and effective phase resets (Figure 8—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by modeling data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Combined stimulation detached the oscillation of the stimulated group for over a second for most stimulus intervals.
claims.source: For most stimulus intervals, combined stimulation detached the oscillation of the stimulated group, which could last for over a second (Figure 8C and D, Figure 8—videos 1 and 2).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by modeling data shown in Figure 8C and D.

claims.claim: The olivary neuropil is characterized by glomeruli comprising a core of dendritic spines coupled by dendrodendritic gap junctions and surrounded by axon terminals.
claims.source: The olivary neuropil is characterized by the so-called glomeruli, which comprise a core of dendritic spines that are coupled by dendrodendritic gap junctions and surrounded by axon terminals (Nĕmecek and Wolff, 1969; Bowman and King, 1973; Sotelo et al., 1974).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Nĕmecek and Wolff, 1969; Bowman and King, 1973; and Sotelo et al., 1974.

claims.claim: Each and every spine of the entire dendritic arbor of olivary neurons in the PO and rostral MAO is innervated by both an inhibitory and excitatory input.
claims.source: Ultrastructural 3D analysis of olivary neurons in the PO and rostral MAO following the use of a combination of intracellular labeling with double or triple labeling of afferents indicates that each and every spine of the entire dendritic arbor is innervated by both an inhibitory and excitatory input (de Zeeuw et al., 1989; De Zeeuw et al., 1990; De Zeeuw, 1990).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to de Zeeuw et al., 1989; De Zeeuw et al., 1990; and De Zeeuw, 1990.

claims.claim: The vast majority of both inhibitory and excitatory afferents terminate onto dendritic spines within the glomeruli.
claims.source: Moreover, the vast majority of both the inhibitory and excitatory afferents terminates onto these spines within the glomeruli.
claims.evidence: This is based on anatomical knowledge from the cited studies.

claims.claim: There are only very few local interneurons in the IO.
claims.source: Given that there are only very few local interneurons in the IO (De Zeeuw, 1990; Fredette et al., 1992), this dominant configuration implies that the interaction between the inhibitory and excitatory inputs onto the electronically coupled spines over time is likely to play an important role in IO function.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to De Zeeuw, 1990 and Fredette et al., 1992.

claims.claim: The impact of CN input on STOs differs substantially from that of MDJ input.
claims.source: The impact of CN input on STOs differs substantially from that of MDJ input.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing CN and MDJ effects shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claims.claim: STOs induced by CN input have on average a smaller Vhyp, possibly due to the flooring effect of HCN channels.
claims.source: STOs induced by CN input have on average a smaller Vhyp, possibly due to the flooring effect of HCN channels, while STOs induced by MDJ input show a more depolarized resting membrane potential.
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental observations and inference about HCN channel properties.

claims.claim: STOs induced by CN input slightly, but significantly, outlast those induced by MDJ input.
claims.source: Despite these differences, the STOs induced by CN input slightly, but significantly, outlast those induced by MDJ input.
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing durations of CN-induced and MDJ-induced oscillations.

claims.claim: The relatively mild phase resetting of MDJ excitation-driven synaptic responses may be related to the conductances recruited during their hyperpolarizing phase.
claims.source: The relatively mild phase resetting and amplitude boost of the MDJ excitation-driven synaptic responses may be related to the conductances that are recruited during their hyperpolarizing phase.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations and knowledge of ion channel properties.

claims.claim: SK and HCN channels mediating the hyperpolarizing component of MDJ responses might be partially inactivated in oscillating neurons during their relatively large membrane depolarizations.
claims.source: These channels might be partially inactivated in oscillating neurons during their relatively large membrane depolarizations (Milligan et al., 2006), reducing the impact of the excitation-mediated Vhyp.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on citation to Milligan et al., 2006 and experimental observations.

claims.claim: Repetitive release of GABA from cerebellar terminals can reduce the level of coupling in olivary glomeruli.
claims.source: For example, repetitive release of the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA from the cerebellar terminals at the olivary spines can reduce the level of coupling (Lang et al., 1996), possibly by shunting the spines with their relatively long necks from the dendrites (Llinas et al., 1974; De Zeeuw et al., 1990; De Zeeuw, 1990), and thereby transiently reduce the strength of the STOs both in vitro (Lefler et al., 2014) and in vivo (Lang, 2002; Bazzigaluppi et al., 2012a; Bazzigaluppi et al., 2012b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Lang et al., 1996; Lefler et al., 2014; Lang, 2002; Bazzigaluppi et al., 2012a; and Bazzigaluppi et al., 2012b.

claims.claim: Enduring entrapment of GABA in the glomeruli for about 60 ms may contribute to long-lasting GABAergic effects.
claims.source: Moreover, given the prominent glial sheaths surrounding the core of innervated and coupled dendrites inside the glomeruli (De Zeeuw et al., 1990; De Zeeuw, 1990) and given the observed long-lasting GABAergic effects on the hyperpolarization of IO neurons in both the experimental and modeling data, enduring entrapment of GABA in the glomeruli for about 60 ms may also contribute.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical knowledge from citations and experimental observations.

claims.claim: The local impact of excitatory glutamatergic afferents on the level of dendrodendritic coupling in the glomeruli varies depending on the duration and frequency of stimulation.
claims.source: Likewise, depending on the duration and frequency of stimulation, the local impact of the excitatory glutamatergic afferents on the level of dendrodendritic coupling in the glomeruli varies (Mathy et al., 2014; Turecek et al., 2014), which in turn will affect the presence and strength of the STOs (De Gruijl et al., 2014b; Negrello et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Mathy et al., 2014; Turecek et al., 2014; De Gruijl et al., 2014b; and Negrello et al., 2019.

claims.claim: When excitation follows inhibition by 50 ms, the STO amplitude boost is small, likely due to depolarization-driven deactivation of HCN channels.
claims.source: We show that when excitation follows inhibition by 50 ms and hits the peak of the hyperpolarizing component of the CN synaptic response, the STO amplitude boost is small, likely as a result of the depolarization-driven deactivation of HCN channels (Bal and McCormick, 1997; Milligan et al., 2006).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental observations and inference supported by citations to Bal and McCormick, 1997 and Milligan et al., 2006.

claims.claim: The most obvious explanation for reduced spike probability at the 50 ms interval is that excitatory synaptic responses are furthest away from spike threshold.
claims.source: The most obvious explanation for the reduced spike probability at this interval is that excitatory synaptic responses are time-wise furthest away from spike threshold given that excitation arrives at the trough of the hyperpolarizing component of the inhibitory response.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations.

claims.claim: Excitation that follows inhibition by 150 ms is most conducive to spike generation because excitation is presented around the peak of the rebound component of the inhibitory response.
claims.source: Conversely, excitation that follows inhibition by 150 ms is most conducive to spike generation, as excitation is presented around the peak of the rebound component of the inhibitory response, which further brings the cell to spike threshold.
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claims.claim: The IO circuitry may allow for phase-based computing that is under control of synaptic inputs from the CN and MDJ.
claims.source: Given that these features were also replicated in our network model and that the size of olivary clusters with sub-cycle phase differences could also be controlled by the inhibitory and excitatory inputs in this model, it is attractive to hypothesize that the IO circuitry may allow for phase-based computing that is under control of the synaptic inputs from the CN and MDJ.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis based on experimental and modeling data.

claims.claim: Such analog computing system can facilitate the generation of a complex array of properly sequenced actions.
claims.source: Such analog computing system can facilitate the generation of a complex array of properly sequenced actions (Holden et al., 2017), in which the sequence of events can be maintained at a variety of speeds or frequencies (Jacobson et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to Holden et al., 2017 and Jacobson et al., 2009.

claims.claim: Different IO clusters may be able to generate olivary oscillations with subtle phase differences, supporting intervals shorter than the cycle period.
claims.source: Indeed, in line with the findings from our olivary network model, systems recordings of complex spike activity in the cerebellar cortex using chronically implanted multi-electrode arrays in freely moving rats indicate that the different IO clusters may be able to generate olivary oscillations with subtle phase differences, supporting intervals shorter than the cycle period, and to maintain these oscillations at a constant phase difference across large global changes in frequency (Jacobson et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Jacobson et al., 2009 and is consistent with modeling results.

claims.claim: Patterns of complex spike activity can be related to ongoing reflex-like behavior and associative sensorimotor behavior.
claims.source: Accordingly, the patterns of complex spike activity can be related to ongoing reflex-like behavior and associative sensorimotor behavior (Welsh et al., 1995; Van Der Giessen et al., 2008; De Gruijl et al., 2014a; Hoogland et al., 2015)
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Welsh et al., 1995; Van Der Giessen et al., 2008; De Gruijl et al., 2014a; and Hoogland et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Disturbing complex spike patterns at the sub-cycle range can affect the latencies of motor behaviors.
claims.source: and disturbing these patterns at the sub-cycle range can affect the latencies of these motor behaviors (Kistler et al., 2002; Van Der Giessen et al., 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Kistler et al., 2002 and Van Der Giessen et al., 2008.

claims.claim: The IO may enable the olivo-cerebellar system to gate temporal patterns at different rates without distortion, facilitating execution of the same behavioral task at different speeds.
claims.source: The IO may thus underlie not only rhythmic activity and synchronization, but also temporal patterning that requires CN-MDJ intervals at various cycle durations and that may enable the olivo-cerebellar system to gate temporal patterns at different rates without distortion, facilitating execution of the same behavioral task at different speeds (Welsh et al., 1995; Ozden et al., 2012; De Gruijl et al., 2014a; Hoogland et al., 2015; Lawrenson et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to Welsh et al., 1995; Ozden et al., 2012; De Gruijl et al., 2014a; Hoogland et al., 2015; and Lawrenson et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Increases and decreases of complex spike activity are critical for cerebellar motor learning by facilitating induction of long-term depression and potentiation at parallel fiber to Purkinje cell synapses.
claims.source: In addition to online control of temporal patterns of complex spike activity that may facilitate ongoing coordination of sensorimotor behavior and/or cognitive functions (Welsh et al., 1995; Hoogland et al., 2015; Romano et al., 2018; Romano et al., 2022), increases and decreases of complex spike activity are also critical for cerebellar motor learning in that they facilitate induction of long-term depression and potentiation at the parallel fiber to Purkinje cell synapses, respectively (Ito and Kano, 1982; Schonewille et al., 2010; Gutierrez-Castellanos et al., 2017)
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Ito and Kano, 1982; Schonewille et al., 2010; and Gutierrez-Castellanos et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Long-term depression and long-term potentiation at Purkinje cell synapses are the dominant forms of plasticity in downbound and upbound microzone modules.
claims.source: Long-term depression and long-term potentiation at the Purkinje cell synapses have been proposed to be the dominant forms of plasticity in the so-called downbound and upbound microzones modules (De Zeeuw, 2021; Voerman et al., 2022), which underlie different forms of motor learning dependent on whether they require decreases and increases in simple spike activity, respectively (Van Der Giessen et al., 2008; ten Brinke et al., 2015; Bina et al., 2022; Yang and Lisberger, 2014; Herzfeld et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to De Zeeuw, 2021; Voerman et al., 2022; Van Der Giessen et al., 2008; ten Brinke et al., 2015; Bina et al., 2022; Yang and Lisberger, 2014; and Herzfeld et al., 2018.

claims.claim: The precise interval between inhibition and excitation of IO neurons determines whether and when complex spike firing frequency will go up or down.
claims.source: Thus, the current finding that the precise interval between inhibition and excitation of IO neurons determines whether and when the complex spike firing frequency will go up or down is probably critical not only for online motor performance, but also for more long-term processes such as motor learning.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

results.result: The manuscript establishes the anatomical and functional context of the inferior olive-cerebellar system, describing how climbing fibers from the inferior olive elicit complex spikes in Purkinje cells and control plasticity mechanisms critical for motor learning and coordination.
results.evaluation: These claims (C1-C3, C7-C15) represent well-established background knowledge supported by extensive citations to prior literature. They provide the foundational context for the study but do not constitute novel findings from the current work.

results.result: The manuscript describes the structural and electrophysiological properties of olivary neurons, including their dendro-dendritic gap junctions, ionic conductances enabling synchronous oscillations, and the unique glomerular architecture where dendritic spines receive both inhibitory and excitatory inputs.
results.evaluation: These claims (C16-C24, C73-C76) are well-supported by extensive citations to prior anatomical and physiological studies. They establish the known properties of the olivary system that motivate the current investigation but represent background knowledge rather than novel findings.

results.result: Characterization of olivary neurons in vitro reveals that 69% display subthreshold oscillations with mean amplitude of 9.52±5.4 mV and frequency of 4.97±1.85 Hz, while oscillating and non-oscillating cells show no significant differences in passive membrane properties.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C38 are directly supported by experimental data with appropriate sample sizes (n=20-100 cells) and statistical analyses. The measurements are consistent with prior literature and provide baseline characterization for the study.

results.result: CN inhibitory input induces GABAAR-mediated biphasic responses (hyperpolarization followed by rebound) that powerfully reset subthreshold oscillations with strong phase resetting (slope = -0.52±0.01), significantly reduce intertrial phase jitter, and boost STO amplitude for multiple post-stimulus cycles.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C48 are well-supported by experimental data including optogenetic stimulation, pharmacological validation with picrotoxin, phase response curve analysis, and quantification across multiple cells. The findings demonstrate robust and reproducible effects of CN input on olivary oscillations.

results.result: MDJ excitatory input produces triphasic responses mediated by AMPA/NMDA receptors followed by HCN/SK channel-mediated hyperpolarization, inducing weaker phase resetting and smaller amplitude changes in STOs compared to CN input, with shorter duration of induced oscillations.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C57 are supported by experimental data using both electrical and optogenetic stimulation, pharmacological validation with CNQX and APV, and statistical comparisons with CN effects. The differential effects of MDJ versus CN input are clearly demonstrated.

results.result: A computational network model of over 1000 olivary neurons successfully reproduces the experimental observations of strong phase resetting following CN stimulation and high variability following MDJ stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C60 are supported by modeling data shown in Figure 4 that accurately recapitulates the experimental phase response curves. The model validation strengthens the mechanistic interpretation of the experimental findings.

results.result: Combined CN-MDJ stimulation at different intervals reveals that the phase response curve slope and intercept vary significantly with timing, with the 150 ms interval producing the steepest slope (-0.69±0.05) and positive ΔΦ-intercept (0.35±0.03), while the 50 ms interval yields minimal STO amplitude (1.83±3.42 mV) compared to maximal amplitude at 150 ms (7.25±3.45 mV).
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C62, C64-C65 are supported by systematic experimental data testing multiple intervals with appropriate statistical analyses (one-way ANOVA). The findings demonstrate interval-dependent effects on phase dynamics and oscillation amplitude.

results.result: The temporal interval between CN inhibition and MDJ excitation critically determines olivary output: excitation ~50 ms after inhibition minimizes spike generation and destabilizes oscillation phase, while excitation ~150 ms after inhibition (one cycle later) optimally drives spiking by riding on powerfully reset subthreshold oscillations, with combined stimulation producing higher spike probability than excitation alone.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C6, C28-C30 represent the central findings of the manuscript, supported by converging evidence from electrophysiology (Figures 5-6), computational modeling (Figures 4, 7-9), and statistical analyses. The ~150 ms optimal interval corresponds to one oscillation cycle and demonstrates precise temporal gating of olivary output.

results.result: Spike probability measurements reveal that combined CN-MDJ stimulation at 150 ms interval produces significantly higher spike probability (0.57±0.3) than either CN alone (0.01±0.03) or MDJ alone (0.22±0.28), while intervals of 50-70 ms yield minimal spiking (Pspike=0), demonstrating bidirectional control of firing.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C70 are supported by direct measurements with appropriate statistical comparisons (one-way ANOVA, p<0.0001). The finding that combined stimulation at optimal timing exceeds either input alone is a key demonstration of temporal integration.

results.result: Network modeling demonstrates that the size of olivary clusters engaged in specific firing patterns depends on the timing and overlap of CN and MDJ inputs, with combined stimulation at one-cycle intervals producing highest rebound amplitude, largest spiking probability, and detachment of stimulated group oscillations lasting over one second.
results.evaluation: Claims C31, C71-C72 are supported by large-scale network simulations (Figures 8-9) showing spatial propagation of temporal effects. The modeling extends single-cell findings to network-level predictions about cluster formation and synchronization.

results.result: The differential impact of CN versus MDJ inputs on STOs is mechanistically explained by differences in recruited conductances, with CN-induced STOs having smaller Vhyp (possibly due to HCN channel flooring) but longer duration, while MDJ-induced weaker phase resetting may result from partial inactivation of SK/HCN channels during membrane depolarizations.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C81 mix experimental observations (C77, C79) with mechanistic inferences (C78, C80-C81) that are plausible but not directly tested. While the proposed mechanisms are consistent with known channel properties and supported by citations, they remain hypothetical without direct pharmacological or voltage-clamp validation.

results.result: The manuscript proposes that repetitive GABA release can reduce gap junction coupling through spine shunting, GABA entrapment in glomeruli may contribute to long-lasting effects (~60 ms), and glutamatergic input variably affects coupling depending on stimulation parameters.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C84 are largely inferential, drawing on prior literature and the current observations but not directly tested in this study. While the proposed mechanisms are plausible and supported by citations, they represent interpretations rather than demonstrated findings.

results.result: The manuscript explains that minimal spike probability at 50 ms interval results from excitation arriving at the trough of CN hyperpolarization (furthest from threshold) with HCN channel deactivation limiting STO boost, while maximal spiking at 150 ms occurs because excitation coincides with the rebound peak.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C87 provide mechanistic explanations for the observed interval-dependent effects, combining experimental observations with inferences about channel states. The explanations are well-supported by the data and consistent with known biophysics, though direct channel measurements were not performed.

results.result: The manuscript proposes that IO circuitry enables phase-based analog computing controlled by CN-MDJ inputs, facilitating generation of properly sequenced actions at variable speeds, with different IO clusters generating oscillations with subtle phase differences that relate to motor behaviors.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C93 represent speculative functional interpretations extending beyond the current data. While supported by citations to behavioral studies and consistent with the findings, these claims about behavioral relevance are not directly tested in this in vitro study.

results.result: The manuscript concludes that precise CN-MDJ intervals determine whether complex spike frequency increases or decreases, which is critical for cerebellar motor learning through differential induction of LTD versus LTP at parallel fiber synapses in downbound versus upbound microzone modules.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C96 connect the current findings to learning mechanisms through extensive citations, but the link to plasticity and learning is not directly demonstrated in this study. The conclusion is plausible and well-motivated but represents an extrapolation requiring future experimental validation.

results.result: Based on theoretical models and anatomical evidence, the manuscript hypothesizes that olivary spike generation is highly sensitive to the temporal interval between inhibitory CN and excitatory MDJ inputs, which was tested using dual-color optogenetics in PO and MAO neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C27 describe the hypothesis and experimental approach. The hypothesis is well-grounded in prior theoretical work and anatomy (supported by citations), and the experimental design appropriately tests this hypothesis using validated techniques.
